items: Have you got a minute?
***Have you got a minute?*** *I have an idea I want to run by you.*
…, if we’ve got a couple of minutes.
*There’s one thing,* ***if we’ve got a couple of minutes****.*
You know how + clause?
***You know how*** *we keep getting calls about putting furniture together?*
I've noticed (that)…
***A lot of*** *new staff* ***said*** *they felt lost.*
Quite a few people said…
I was thinking, what if we + V (past)?
***I was thinking, what if we made*** *some short how-to videos?*
What I’m suggesting is + N
***What I’m suggesting is*** *a buddy system.*
Maybe we could + V
***Maybe we could*** *talk to the new staff after a month.*
would / could / might + V
*Customers* ***would*** *get help straight away. We* ***might*** *also get fewer returns.*
We’d have more time for + N
***We’d have more time for*** *difficult problems.*
That way, + clause
***That way****, new staff always know who to ask.*
Nothing too… / just / only
***Nothing too formal****,* ***just*** *someone to show them the ropes.*
That’s why I’d like to start small.
***That’s why I’d like to start small****, with a one-month trial.*
I can look into it/I can find out.
*Good question. I haven’t thought about that yet.* ***I can find out.***
Let me think about it and get back to you.
***I’m not sure yet. Let me think about it and get back to you.***

lesson.label: 🧠 Brainstorming questions (Câu hỏi nên nghĩ trước buổi học)
items: Have you ever **suggested a new idea at work or school?** What happened?
Do you **feel nervous sharing an idea with your manager? Why?**
If you could change **one small thing about your workplace,** what would it be?
What makes people **say “yes” to a new idea?**

lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. Can I run something by you?
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Emma works in customer service at an online furniture shop. She catches her manager, Rachel, after the weekly meeting.*
lines: Rachel, **have you got a minute**? I’ve had an idea I wanted to **run by you**.
**You know how** we **keep getting** calls about putting furniture together? I counted last week, and it was almost half of all our calls.
Half? I knew it was a lot, but **I didn’t realise** it was that bad.

Yeah, it **takes up a lot of time**, and most calls are about the same few products. So **I was thinking**, **what if we made** some short **how-to videos** for those? We could send the link with every order.
So customers could just watch a video instead of **waiting on the phone**.

Exactly. They’d **get help straight away**, and we’d have more time for **difficult problems**. We might also get **fewer returns**. A lot of people send things back because they don’t know how to put them together.
**That makes sense.** But videos are expensive, and we don’t have **a big budget**.
I don’t think it would cost much. Jack made videos at his old company. With a good phone and some simple editing, we could **do it ourselves**.
I think we could make the first three videos **in about two weeks**. We can **still do our normal work** at the same time.
And what if people still call?
Some people will, **for sure**. That’s why I’d like to **start small**, with **a one-month trial** for three products. Then we can **check** the number of calls and see if it **makes a difference**.
OK, I think it’s **worth a try**. Can you send me a short email with the numbers? I’ll **talk to** the director **about it** on Thursday.
Great, I’ll send it today. **Thanks for listening.**

lesson.title: 2. Sharing an idea in a meeting
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Nathan works in HR at a tech company. At the end of the monthly team meeting, his manager, Claire, asks if anyone has anything else to discuss.*
lines: OK, I think that’s everything **on the agenda**. Anything else before we finish?
Actually, there’s one thing, **if we’ve got a couple of minutes**. It’s about **new staff**.

So, in the last survey, a lot of new staff said they **felt lost** in their first month. They didn’t know **who to ask** when they **had a problem**. Two people who left this year said the same thing.
**I know how that feels.** When I started, I spent two days trying to find out how to book a meeting room. I was too shy to ask.

Right. So **what I’m suggesting is a buddy system**. Each new person would have a “buddy”, someone from their team who’s been here for a while. **Nothing too formal**, just someone to **show them around** and have lunch with in the first week.
I like the idea, but who’s got time for that? We’re all really busy.
That’s fair. It would only be people who want to do it, and it’s maybe an hour or two a week. Buddies just need to **help out** when new staff have a question.
**I’d be happy to do it**, to be honest.
Would buddies **get anything for it**, though?
**Good question.** I haven’t thought about that yet. Maybe a lunch voucher or something?
And how would we know if it’s working?
Hmm, I’m not sure yet. Maybe we could talk to the new staff after a month? Let me think about it and **get back to you**.
OK. I think it’s **worth a try**. Let’s **try it** with the next two or three people who join and **see how it goes**.
Great. I’ll write a short plan and send it to everyone by Friday.
Perfect. Thanks, Nathan. Right, I think **that’s it for today**.
vocab: **if we’ve got a couple of minutes**
/ɪf wiːv ɡɒt ə ˈkʌp.əl əv ˈmɪn.ɪts/

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check (conversation)
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Lily works in a small bakery. Before the shop opens, she talks to her manager, Tom.
bank: takes up a lot of time
lines: Tom, have you got a minute? I've had an idea I wanted to {run by you}.
You know how customers {keep calling} us to order birthday cakes? It {takes up a lot of time}, and sometimes we can't answer because we're too busy.
Yes, I know. Last week, one customer had to {wait on the phone} for ten minutes.
Exactly. So I was thinking, what if we made a simple order form on our Facebook page? Customers could choose the cake, the size and the date.
Hmm, {That makes sense}. But we don't have a big {budget} for a website.
We don't need a website. A Facebook form is free, and we could {do it ourselves}.
And what if some customers still call?
Some people will, for sure. That's why I'd like to {start small}, with a {one-month trial}. Then we can count the phone calls and see if it makes a difference.
OK, I think it's {worth a try}. Let's start next week.

homework.title: Part 2: Vocab check (sentences)
homework.instructions: Complete each sentence with a phrase from the box. Use each phrase once. You don't need to change the form of the words.
lines: Before we finish, is there anything else {on the agenda}?
I'm not sure what time the meeting is. I'll check and {get back to you}.
Don't worry about your first day. Sarah will {show you around} the office.
“Can I tell the team about my idea?” “Sure, {go for it}.”
“I was so nervous on my first day.” “{I know how that feels}. I was nervous too.”
Let's try the new timetable for two weeks and {see how it goes}.
When I started this job, I didn't know {who to ask} when I had a problem.
He was {too shy} to ask questions in the meeting, so he stayed quiet.
If you need anything, just ask. I'm always happy to {help out}.
OK, thanks, everyone. I think {that's it for today}.

homework.title: Part 3: Listening
homework.intro: Anna and Jack are friends. They're having coffee after work. Listen, then do Parts A and B.
homework.podcast: 🎧 Anna & Jack: the new working hours

script.text: So, did you talk to your manager about your idea?
Yes, this morning. I was really nervous, but it went well.
Remind me, what was the idea?
I asked if our team could start work at ==eight== and finish at ==four==, instead of nine to five.
Because the ==traffic is terrible at half past eight==. It takes me an hour to get to work. If I leave home earlier, it only takes ==twenty minutes==.
That makes sense. What did your manager say?
At first, she wasn't sure. She said, ==“What if a client calls at half past four and nobody's there?”==
Yeah. So I said not everyone needs to change. Some people can still work nine to five, so there's always someone in the office until five.
Smart. So did she say yes?
Not completely. She wants to start small. ==Three people can try it for one month==, and then she'll check if it's working.
That's great! Are you one of the three?
Yes, I start next ==Monday==. I'm so happy. ==I'll have more time with my kids== in the afternoon.
That sounds amazing. Maybe I should talk to my boss too.
Go for it. Just explain the problem first, and suggest a short trial. It's much easier for managers to say yes.

questions.q: What did Jack ask his manager?
options: If he could work from home
If he could change his working hours
If he could work fewer days a week
questions.why: “I asked if our team could start work at eight and finish at four, instead of nine to five.”

questions.q: Why does Jack want this change?
options: He wants to avoid the heavy traffic.
He wants to earn more money.
questions.why: “The traffic is terrible at half past eight.”

questions.q: How long will it take Jack to get to work if he leaves home earlier?
questions.why: “If I leave home earlier, it only takes twenty minutes.”

questions.q: What was the manager worried about?
options: Nobody would be in the office if a client called late.
Jack might arrive late for work.
The team might not finish their work.
questions.why: “What if a client calls at half past four and nobody's there?”

options: Everyone can start work at eight.
A small group can try the new hours for a month.
questions.why: “Three people can try it for one month.”

options: He can spend more time with his children.
He doesn't have to go to the office any more.
His manager gave him a new job.
questions.why: “I'll have more time with my kids in the afternoon.”

homework.instructions: Choose ONE option and record yourself speaking. You are the only speaker.
